rationale: Patients recruited with de novo parkinsonism underwent clinical screening and structural MRI with follow-up. The analysis focused on progression of brain atrophy in early diagnosed Parkinson disease without cognitive impairment. Motor symptoms and medication timing characterize the cohort. Brain volume change does not measure a dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The paper reviews diagnostic criteria and treatment evidence for Parkinson dementia and psychosis, including visual illusions, hallucinations and medication-related risks. It compares clinical trial and practice findings on different agents. The review provides no new dietary intervention or episode-frequency estimate after dried figs.

The authors pool case-control evidence for DRD2 and DRD3 polymorphisms and susceptibility to Parkinson disease. The outcome is genetic association with diagnostic status. That outcome cannot identify a dried fig or hallucination-frequency effect.

Drosophila expressing an LRRK2 variant underwent retinal and brain visual-response recordings. The investigators measured contrast responses and visual gain, including comparisons using LRRK2 kinase inhibitors in fly food. A stimulus-evoked electrophysiological response is distinct from hallucinations in humans. No dried fig preparation was evaluated.

The review compares cognition, dementia timing, visual experiences and treatment in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. Prior cohorts describe different time relations to motor onset and medication. The review does not test dried figs or measure a new visual episode rate.

Resting functional connectivity was measured in 16 individuals with fluctuating dementia with Lewy bodies and 17 age-matched controls. The paper discusses overlap of hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations. Its primary contrasts concern functional connectivity and cognitive fluctuation rather than response to food or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The authors examine the NIMH Research Domain Criteria framework, comparing explanations for hallucinations across clinical and nonclinical groups. The worked example emphasizes auditory verbal hallucinations. A conceptual extension to other modalities cannot establish the effect of dried fig intake on visual hallucination frequency in Parkinson disease.

The investigators compare 34 monoallelic GBA Parkinson patients with 60 comparison patients. Persistent hallucinations were operationalized by a UPDRS thought-disorder rating above one over more than six months. The reported hazard ratio was 5.0 with p=0.01. Table 1 shows nine and four individuals meeting that sustained threshold respectively. The time-to-criterion event uses a composite item and persistence across visits, not counted visual episodes. The study supplies no dietary exposure comparison.

The study analyzes GABA-A receptor autoantibodies using patient samples and laboratory methods. One clinical history describes a visual hallucination during autoimmune encephalitis with seizures and delirium. That observation is useful for differential context. It supplies no dried fig challenge or Parkinson visual outcome.

This review of dopamine-transporter SPECT compares Parkinson disease and other parkinsonian syndromes, including dementia with Lewy bodies. Visual hallucinations figure in clinical differential diagnosis and in cited studies. The imaging review evaluates neither fig intake nor episode frequency after a culinary exposure.

The review considers insomnia, daytime sleepiness, REM sleep behavior disorder and other sleep disturbances in Parkinson disease. Medication effects and hallucinations are discussed in relation to sleep and treatment. The review provides no measured fig exposure or clinical visual episode comparison.

The paper compares sleep outcomes across multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy and other atypical syndromes. Visual hallucinations are mentioned as clinical features and in cited medication intolerance. Sleep observations and case citations do not establish a dried fig or idiopathic Parkinson episode rate.

The cognitive screening study compares MMSE and MoCA scores in 304 Parkinson patients. It tests the sensitivity and specificity of cognitive-domain items in assessing dementia. The design does not measure dried fig consumption or hallucination frequency.

The article synthesizes pharmacological, behavioral and imaging results on serotonergic hallucinogens. Its laboratory and human source studies apply to specific agents and perceptual mechanisms. Acute pharmacological perceptual effects cannot establish a clinical Parkinson episode rate for dried figs.

PINK1-mutant and wild-type fruit flies received individual botanical preparations, a five-herb combination, levodopa or comparison feed. The preparations were a commercial Mucuna pruriens powder, Withania somnifera, Centella asiatica, Sida cordifolia and Bacopa monnieri. Bacopa improved mutant climbing but worsened wild-type climbing. Centella also reduced wild-type climbing, and the other individual herbs yielded no significant change versus untreated flies in the reported comparisons. Neither the tested preparations nor the climbing endpoint matches dried figs and clinical visual hallucination frequency.

The study follows 47 mild cognitive impairment participants and compares EEG patterns with subsequent dementia classification. Visual hallucination status is recorded in the clinical tables along with REM sleep behavior and cognition. EEG measures and symptom presence serve diagnostic prediction rather than exposure assignment or visual event frequency in Parkinson disease.

The study examines associations between cognitive performance and resting-state functional network connectivity in Parkinson disease. Network and cognitive contrasts are the primary measures. No dietary assignment or visual hallucination episode count by dried fig exposure is reported.

The commentary traces the original electrical stimulation case and related cortical-network findings on evoked visual scenes and déjà vu. It discusses a report in an epilepsy-surgery setting and separates it from other network hypotheses. There is no new patient cohort, food exposure or count of spontaneous Parkinson visual events.

The study compares thalamic connectivity and microstructure in dementia with Lewy bodies, focusing on fluctuating cognition and alertness. A visual hallucination or parkinsonism can satisfy part of the clinical classification, but the reported analysis concerns cognitive fluctuation and imaging. No food challenge is reported.

The review synthesizes research on cortical spreading depression in migraine aura, vascular and trigeminal theories, imaging and animal experiments. A slowly progressing visual aura and neurophysiological depolarization are separate from formed hallucinations in Parkinson disease. There is no fig trial or measured food-associated visual symptom frequency.

The paper pools association studies of seven GIGYF2 polymorphisms and Parkinson susceptibility. Genotype and diagnostic status comparisons do not measure dietary exposure or a visual hallucination rate.

The review traces Lewy body pathology and contrasts clinical classifications of Parkinson disease, Parkinson dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies. Its references to visual hallucinations support differences in diagnostic presentation. There is no dietary comparison or series of visual episode counts following fig consumption.

The study compares phosphorylated alpha-synuclein inclusions in skin specimens in Parkinson disease and other parkinsonian presentations. Its clinical context includes visual hallucinations as a feature of Lewy body disease. The measured diagnostic tissue endpoint cannot establish an effect on food-associated visual episodes.

The study compares cerebral amyloid tracer uptake in posterior cortical atrophy and amnestic Alzheimer disease. Visual hallucinations appear in the syndrome's clinical description. The material comparison concerns imaging patterns and separate diagnoses, with no measured dried fig exposure or Parkinson episode frequency.

The review describes genetic and diagnostic forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, movement symptoms and associated neuropsychiatric findings. It concerns disease phenotypes and imaging or clinical assessment. This clinical context supplies no fig comparison or food-timed visual hallucination count in Parkinson disease.

The paper tests optical stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus in a rat model and reports microdialysis measurements of striatal dopamine and glutamate. These are laboratory neurotransmitter outcomes. The experiment does not administer a fig preparation or measure clinical visual hallucinations.

The authors describe how to evaluate cognitive complaints in older people and distinguish different patterns of dementia and delirium. Visual hallucinations occur in evidence-based differential diagnosis. This practice review supplies no original dietary intervention or measure of Parkinson visual episode change after dried figs.

The review synthesizes sleep attacks and sudden sleep onset reported during dopaminergic therapy. Its cases include visual and auditory hallucinations coded separately among co-occurring symptoms. The primary outcome is sleep attacks. Co-occurring case reports, with concurrent medication and variable ascertainment, do not establish a food-associated visual episode rate.
